## The Full-Cycle AI Scientist: End-to-End Research Automation {#sec-full-cycle}

### The Audacious Vision: AI Scientist v1

In August 2024, researchers at Sakana AI, in collaboration with the University of British Columbia, published a paper that pushed the boundaries of what anyone had demonstrated an LLM-based system could do. [**The AI Scientist**]{style="color: #047857;"} ([Lu et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292)) was not an agent for one stage of research. It was a system that attempted the entire scientific process, from brainstorming a research idea to producing a finished, formatted research paper, without any human involvement in between. And it did so for a total cost of less than fifteen dollars per paper.

To understand why this was striking, consider what the full research process normally requires. A human researcher needs to: (1) identify a promising research direction by reading existing literature, (2) formulate a specific, testable hypothesis, (3) design an experiment to test it, (4) write the code to implement the experiment, (5) run the experiments and collect results, (6) create figures and tables to present the results, (7) write a paper explaining the motivation, methods, results, and conclusions, and (8) revise the paper based on peer feedback. Each of these steps requires different skills: creativity, domain expertise, programming ability, statistical reasoning, clear writing. The AI Scientist attempted all of them.

The system operated in three main phases, followed by an automated evaluation step:

**Phase 1: Idea Generation.** Given a starting code template in one of three topic areas (diffusion modeling, transformer-based language modeling, or learning dynamics), the system used an LLM to brainstorm a list of potential research questions. Each idea was filtered for novelty by polling the Semantic Scholar API to check whether similar work already existed. Ideas that passed the filter were ranked, and the top candidate was selected for investigation.

**Phase 2: Experimental Iteration.** The selected idea was translated into code modifications. Here was the critical constraint of v1: the system started from a **human-authored code template**, a working baseline implementation written by the paper's authors. The AI Scientist modified this template to implement the new idea, changing model architectures, modifying training procedures, and adding evaluation metrics. It then ran the modified code, producing training logs and metrics, executed multiple runs with different configurations, and iterated on the code based on results. This tight loop of code modification, execution, and refinement was a single integrated phase, not two separate ones. The process was closer to how graduate students work (forking a professor's code and modifying it) than writing experiments from scratch.

**Phase 3: Paper Write-up.** Using the experimental results, the system wrote a complete paper in LaTeX: abstract, introduction (including motivation and relation to prior work), methods, results, discussion, and conclusion. The system used Semantic Scholar's API to search for relevant prior work and generate a literature review, producing citations to real papers. It generated publication-quality figures (training curves, comparison tables, ablation studies) using matplotlib.

**Automated Peer Review.** As a separate evaluation step, the AI Scientist also played the role of *reviewer*: it evaluated the finished paper using a structured rubric (similar to those used by ML conferences like NeurIPS and ICML), scoring the paper on novelty, significance, soundness, and clarity. This automated review served as both a quality filter and a signal for which papers were worth improving through additional revision cycles.

::: {.exercise-fillin}

The AI Scientist v1 operates in three main phases plus a separate evaluation step. Fill in the missing phase:

1. **Idea Generation** — brainstorm research questions, filter for novelty via Semantic Scholar
2. {B|A: Literature Review and Citation — search for and synthesize relevant prior work|B: Experimental Iteration — modify code template, run experiments, analyze results, iterate|C: Hypothesis Refinement — use automated review to iteratively improve the research question}
3. **Paper Write-up** — write a complete LaTeX paper with introduction, methods, results, discussion
4. *Automated Peer Review* — evaluate the paper using a structured rubric (separate evaluation step)

::: {.fillin-feedback}
**Correct: B (Experimental Iteration).** After idea generation, the system enters a tight loop of modifying the code template, running experiments, analyzing results, and iterating, all as a single integrated phase. Option A (Literature Review) is part of Phase 3 (Paper Write-up), where the system uses Semantic Scholar's API. Option C (Hypothesis Refinement) is not a separate phase; the system commits to one idea after Phase 1.
:::

:::

### What Fifteen Dollars Buys You

The outputs of the AI Scientist were, by any measure, a mixed bag. Honestly examining both the successes and failures is more informative than celebrating the headline.

**The successes were genuine.** The system produced papers on topics like "Adaptive Dual-Scale Denoising" (a modification to diffusion model training) and "Grokking Accelerated: Layer-wise Learning Rates for Transformer Generalization" (an investigation of how different learning rate schedules affect the sudden-generalization phenomenon known as grokking). These papers had coherent arguments, real experimental results, and conclusions that followed from the data. The ideas, while not earth-shattering, represented plausible incremental contributions of the kind that populate many workshop papers and conference submissions. The automated reviewer achieved *near-human performance* in evaluating paper quality: on ICLR 2022 review data, its ratings achieved 65% balanced accuracy, compared to 66% for human reviewers, suggesting that LLMs are genuinely competent at evaluating research quality, even if their research *generation* is more uneven.

**The failures were equally genuine, and instructive.** The literature reviews were often superficial: the system cited real papers but did not engage deeply with their findings or correctly position the new work relative to them. The experiment execution sometimes produced buggy results that the system failed to detect, including incorrect baselines or results that looked plausible but were artifacts of implementation mistakes. The system occasionally fabricated experimental details in the paper text: for example, claiming experiments were run on V100 GPUs when H100s were actually used, or guessing the PyTorch version rather than checking. (Notably, the *numerical* results in tables were verified to exactly match the experimental logs; the hallucinations were in the surrounding prose descriptions of experimental setup, not in the data itself.) Most seriously, the system occasionally made claims in the paper that were not fully supported by the experimental evidence.

These failure modes are not crippling, but they are structurally important. They reveal a telling asymmetry: the *format* of scientific communication (the flow of a paper, the structure of an argument, the visual design of figures) is something LLMs can reproduce competently, while the *substance* of scientific reasoning (ensuring claims are supported, identifying subtle errors, positioning contributions accurately in the existing literature) is something they handle unevenly at best.

::: {.exercise-mcq correct="B"}

The AI Scientist's automated reviewer achieves near-human accuracy at predicting paper quality, while paper *generation* is more uneven. Why is evaluation easier than generation for LLM-based systems?

- The reviewer uses a more powerful LLM than the paper generator.
- Evaluation requires checking focused, answerable properties (Are claims supported? Are baselines appropriate?), while generation requires simultaneously satisfying all quality properties while constructing a novel argument, a harder combinatorial challenge.
- The reviewer is fine-tuned on human review data, while the paper generator uses only zero-shot prompting.
- Evaluation is a classification task (good vs. bad), which LLMs are fundamentally better at than open-ended text generation.

::: {.feedback-correct}
Correct. The asymmetry is structural, not about model choice. A reviewer can decompose the task into focused checks: "Is claim X supported by evidence Y?" Each check is answerable in isolation. The generator must satisfy *all* properties simultaneously while constructing a novel argument. This is the same asymmetry that explains why chess engines could evaluate positions before they could play at master level.
:::

::: {.feedback-incorrect}
Option A is wrong: the same underlying LLM is used for both. Option C is wrong: the reviewer uses a structured rubric, not fine-tuned weights. Option D oversimplifies: review is not binary classification but structured scoring across multiple dimensions. The correct answer is B: evaluation decomposes into focused checks, while generation is a combinatorial challenge.
:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Think Hard: Why does the AI Scientist's automated reviewer achieve near-human performance while the paper generation has significant shortcomings?"}
The asymmetry between good evaluation and mediocre generation is not accidental. It reflects a well-understood principle in both AI and human cognition: *evaluation is easier than generation.*

To evaluate a paper, the reviewer can check specific, concrete properties: Are the claims supported by the evidence? Are the baselines appropriate? Is the writing clear? Each of these checks is a focused, answerable question. To *generate* a paper, the system must simultaneously satisfy all of these properties while constructing a novel argument from scratch. That is a much harder combinatorial challenge.

The parallel to other domains is instructive. Chess engines could evaluate positions effectively long before they could play at a master level. Human readers can identify flawed arguments much more easily than they can construct sound ones. For the AI Scientist, the practical takeaway is that the automated reviewer is genuinely useful as a quality filter, even though the paper generator needs significant improvement. In a practical workflow, this asymmetry could be put to use: generate *draft* papers rapidly and cheaply, then use AI review (combined with human review) to identify and fix the drafts' shortcomings.
:::

### From Templates to Agentic Search: AI Scientist v2

The most fundamental limitation of AI Scientist v1 was its dependence on human-authored code templates. The system could modify and extend existing code, but it could not start from a blank slate. This constraint meant that the set of possible experiments was bounded by what the template-writers had anticipated. The system could explore variations within a pre-defined space but could not venture into truly novel experimental designs requiring fundamentally different code architectures.

**AI Scientist v2** ([Yamada, Lange, Lu et al., Sakana AI, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08066)) addressed this limitation through a technique called **progressive agentic tree search.** Instead of starting from a monolithic code template, v2 eliminates the need for human-authored templates entirely. The system begins from an AI-generated research idea with no pre-existing code, and builds experiments incrementally through a tree-structured exploration process:

1. The system starts by generating a *minimal working prototype* from scratch (just enough code to establish feasibility and correctness) rather than modifying a human-provided template.
2. It generates multiple possible *next steps* (add a specific architectural component, implement a particular loss function, introduce a data augmentation technique), each representing a branch in the tree.
3. Each branch is executed and evaluated using a best-first search strategy where an LLM assesses candidates, and the most promising branches are expanded further.
4. This process continues until the system has built a complete, functioning experiment, constructed incrementally from components rather than adapted from a template.

This progressive construction approach has two advantages over the template-based approach. (a) It enables a much wider range of experimental designs, because the system is not constrained by the template-writer's assumptions. (b) The tree-search structure provides a natural mechanism for handling failures: if a particular code addition causes bugs or degrades performance, the system can backtrack to a previous checkpoint and try a different branch.

The milestone achievement of v2 was that a paper generated entirely by the system, with no human-authored code template and minimal human involvement, was **accepted at a peer-reviewed venue** (the ICLR 2025 "I Can't Believe It's Not Better" workshop) after standard peer review, receiving scores of 6, 7, and 6. To the best of public knowledge, this was the first time an AI-generated scientific paper passed standard peer review. The paper was subsequently withdrawn before publication, per a pre-arrangement with the ICLR organizers, but the acceptance itself through the standard review process was the demonstrated milestone. The significance of this achievement is genuine but contested. It demonstrates that AI systems can produce work that clears the quality bar of peer review at a workshop venue. But it also raises questions about the quality threshold of workshop reviews and whether the paper represents genuine scientific contribution or sophisticated imitation of the form.

### Execution-Grounded Research: Learning from Experimental Feedback

AI Scientist v1 and v2 both generate ideas and execute them, but they treat each paper as a standalone attempt. A natural question is whether the system can *learn from its own experimental results* to generate better ideas over time. **Execution-Grounded Automated AI Research** ([Si et al., 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14525)) directly investigates this question at scale. The team built an automated executor that implements LLM-generated research ideas as code, launches parallel GPU experiments, and feeds the results back to the idea generator.

Si et al. studied two realistic AI research environments: LLM pre-training (optimizing nanoGPT training recipes) and post-training (improving GRPO-based reinforcement learning). The system sampled hundreds of ideas from frontier LLMs, implemented each as code, ran the experiments, and collected performance metrics. Two learning algorithms were compared for improving idea generation from this execution feedback.

::: {.exercise-predict correct="A"}

Si et al. (2026) built a system that implements LLM-generated research ideas as code, runs experiments, and feeds results back to improve idea generation. They compared evolutionary search (variation + selection + recombination) with reinforcement learning from execution reward. Which approach performed better?

- Evolutionary search dominated: it found ideas that significantly outperformed baselines, while RL suffered from diversity collapse (converging on safe, mediocre ideas).
- RL dominated: gradient-based optimization found better ideas faster.
- Both performed comparably: the search algorithm mattered less than the quality of the underlying LLM.

::: {.predict-reveal}
**The answer is A.** Evolutionary search found a post-training method improving accuracy from 48.0% to 69.4% and a pre-training recipe that nearly halved training time. RL suffered from *diversity collapse*: it improved average reward but not the upper bound, because models converged on safe, simple ideas rather than exploring novel directions. RL optimizes for *expected* performance, which penalizes high-variance exploration. But the most valuable scientific ideas are precisely the high-variance ones.
:::

:::

**Evolutionary search** proved remarkably sample-efficient. Starting from a population of LLM-generated ideas, the system applied variation (mutating successful ideas), selection (keeping top performers), and recombination (merging elements from different successful approaches). Within just ten search epochs, evolutionary search found a post-training method that significantly outperformed the GRPO baseline (69.4% vs. 48.0% accuracy), and a pre-training recipe that cut nanoGPT training time nearly in half (19.7 minutes vs. 35.9 minutes). These are not trivial improvements; they represent the kind of gains that would earn a workshop paper if discovered by a human researcher.

**Reinforcement learning from execution reward**, by contrast, suffered from a striking failure mode: *diversity collapse.* The RL-trained ideator model learned to improve its *average* reward (generating ideas that were more consistently decent) but not its *upper bound* (generating ideas that were occasionally brilliant). The model converged on safe, simple ideas: variations on approaches it already knew worked, not explorations of novel algorithmic directions. This finding resonates with a broader pattern. RL optimizes for expected performance, which penalizes high-variance exploration. But the most valuable scientific ideas are precisely the high-variance ones: risky hypotheses that usually fail but occasionally produce breakthroughs.

The deeper implication is that evolutionary search (which maintains a diverse population and explicitly combines elements from different lineages) may be a better algorithmic framework for scientific ideation than RL (which collapses toward a single policy). Google's AI co-scientist uses an iterative "generate, evaluate, refine" framework; AlphaEvolve ([Novikov et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13131)) uses evolutionary search over code. The convergent adoption of evolutionary methods across independent research groups suggests a genuine architectural insight: scientific creativity requires maintaining diversity. Evolution is a better mechanism for that than gradient-based optimization.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common Misconception: The AI Scientist can replace human researchers"}
The headline ("AI system writes scientific papers for $15 that pass peer review") invites a straightforward conclusion: human researchers are about to be replaced. But the benchmark data tells a different story. When AI Scientist and similar systems are evaluated on standardized scientific task benchmarks ([DiscoveryBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01725), [ScienceAgentBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.05080)), they solve only 25-42% of tasks. The papers they produce pass review at some venues but would likely be rejected at top-tier conferences with more rigorous evaluation criteria. Their literature reviews are shallow, their experimental designs conventional, and their claims sometimes overstate the evidence. What The AI Scientist demonstrates is not that human researchers are replaceable, but that the *mechanical* aspects of research (writing code, running experiments, formatting papers) can be automated. That automation frees human researchers to focus on the *intellectual* aspects: choosing important problems, designing creative experiments, interpreting results in context, and identifying genuinely novel contributions. The "$15 per paper" is real, but the intellectual value of a paper cannot be measured in dollars.
:::

### The Human-in-the-Loop Alternative: Agent Laboratory

If The AI Scientist represents the "full autonomy" philosophy (remove the human entirely and let the AI drive the process end-to-end), then [Agent Laboratory]{style="color: #047857;"} ([Schmidgall et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.04227)) represents the "augmented researcher" philosophy: keep the human in the loop at strategic decision points and let the AI handle the time-consuming mechanical work.

We covered Agent Laboratory's three-stage architecture in @sec-experimentation, but its relevance here is in the *comparison* with The AI Scientist. Both systems aim to produce research outputs; they differ in *where the human sits.*

| Aspect | AI Scientist (v1/v2) | Agent Laboratory |
|--------|---------------------|-----------------|
| **Human involvement** | None (fully autonomous) | Feedback at each stage gate |
| **Starting point** | Code template (v1) or minimal infrastructure (v2) | Research topic |
| **Output** | Complete paper | Research report |
| **Cost reduction** | ~$15/paper (from ~$100k human cost) | 84% reduction vs. human baseline |
| **Quality assurance** | Automated peer review | Human feedback + automated checks |
| **Success on benchmarks** | 25-34% (DiscoveryBench/ScienceAgentBench) | Higher quality per output (human-reviewed) |
| **Key advantage** | Speed, cost, scale | Quality, reliability, trust |
| **Key limitation** | Unreliable quality, hallucination risk | Requires human time at each gate |

The "84% cost reduction" finding is significant because it quantifies the practical value proposition of the augmentation approach. If a fully autonomous system produces outputs that require extensive human review and correction afterward (effectively undoing much of the automation), the net time savings may be less than a system that incorporates human feedback during the process and produces higher-quality outputs from the start. Agent Laboratory's finding that "human feedback significantly improves quality" is both unsurprising and important: it confirms that the most productive near-term configuration is not "AI replaces human" but "AI and human collaborate, with each contributing their comparative advantage."

### Real-World Validation: From Hypothesis to Experiment

The most compelling evidence for AI agents' potential in science comes not from papers about AI writing papers, but from cases where AI-generated hypotheses were validated through real-world experiments by human researchers.

**FutureHouse's [Robin]{style="color: #4F46E5;"}** ([Ghareeb, Chang et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13400)) autonomously discovered a drug repurposing candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (dAMD). The system used Crow and Falcon (literature search agents of different depth, both built on PaperQA2) to search thousands of ophthalmology and pharmacology papers, identifying the hypothesis that enhancing RPE phagocytosis could provide therapeutic benefit for dAMD. Through iterative rounds of hypothesis generation and experimental validation (with human researchers executing the physical experiments), Robin identified ripasudil, a ROCK inhibitor already used clinically for glaucoma, as a novel therapeutic candidate. Follow-up RNA-seq analysis by Finch revealed upregulation of ABCA1, a critical lipid efflux pump, suggesting a specific molecular mechanism. All hypotheses, experimental designs, data analyses, and figures were generated autonomously by Robin.

[Google's AI Co-Scientist]{style="color: #047857;"} ([Gottweis and Natarajan, 2025](https://research.google/blog/accelerating-scientific-breakthroughs-with-an-ai-co-scientist/)) went one step further: its hypotheses were not just proposed but *validated in vitro.* For acute myeloid leukemia (AML), the system's six-agent framework (Generation, Reflection, Ranking, Evolution, Proximity, and Meta-review) proposed specific drug targets: existing drugs that might be repurposed for AML treatment. Collaborating biologists then tested these predictions in laboratory cell cultures (multiple AML cell lines), confirming that the suggested drugs inhibit tumor viability at clinically relevant concentrations. The AML result is biological, not computational; it was *inspired by* computational prediction. The AI did not run the experiments; human biologists did. But the hypothesis (the crucial intellectual contribution) originated from the AI system.

The dAMD and AML validations are important because they cross the boundary from *in silico* (in the computer) to *in vitro* (in the laboratory). A paper written by an AI can be assessed for its formatting and argumentation, but a hypothesis validated in the lab can be assessed for its *scientific truth.* The dAMD and AML results demonstrate that AI systems can generate hypotheses that are not just plausible-sounding but *experimentally correct:* the outputs correspond to physical reality.

::: {.callout-note title="Think Hard: If AI Scientist v2 can produce papers that pass peer review, does this reveal more about the AI's capability or about the limitations of peer review?"}
The question is genuinely important, and the honest answer is "both." On the AI side, the fact that a system can produce a paper with a coherent argument, real experimental results, and a correct format is a genuine capability achievement. On the peer review side, the result highlights three well-documented limitations of the review process:

- Reviewers are often overstretched (reading 5-10 papers in a few weeks alongside their own research)
- Reviews are sometimes superficial (checking that the paper "looks right" rather than deeply verifying claims)
- Review criteria at many venues emphasize novelty and presentation over rigorous verification

A paper that has a correct structure, plausible experiments, and incremental results can pass review even if its literature review is shallow, its claims slightly overstated, or its code contains subtle bugs. Workshop and lower-tier venues are especially susceptible. The AI Scientist's achievement is real but needs context: the system has learned to clear the *minimum quality bar* of published research, which is not the same as producing the highest-quality research. The practical implication is that AI-generated papers should be treated like papers from any other source: read critically, with claims verified against the evidence and methods examined for soundness.
:::

**Where Maya stands after this section.** Maya can now see the full spectrum of approaches. At one extreme, The AI Scientist offers complete autonomy: she could feed in her drug repurposing topic and potentially receive a draft paper, but she would need to verify every claim, check every analysis, and validate every citation. At the other extreme, Agent Laboratory offers structured augmentation: the AI would accelerate her literature review, help design and run computational experiments, and draft sections of her report. She would provide feedback at each stage, maintaining quality control. In between, Robin and Google's AI co-scientist offer targeted autonomy in hypothesis generation. They might identify drug repurposing candidates that she would not have found through manual literature review, but she would still need to validate them through her own computational and experimental work. Given the stakes of her research (false positives waste months of wet-lab effort), Maya would likely choose the Agent Laboratory approach for her next project. She would supplement her literature review with PaperQA2 or Robin to surface AI-generated candidates that she evaluates herself.
